Generate a synthetic panel of individual incomes for public release.
No actual data, previously saved analytical results, or parameters estimated from actual data are used.
The distributions and parameters below are chosen for this computational example and do not guarantee replication of the empirical results or the validity of the model.

Save the income panel `sample_size_tb` and growth data `sample_growth_tb` in `qs2` format in `../income_board_replicate/`, matching the columns, types, and units read by the analysis code in 02–11.
Income in yen is stored as `main_var`, and birth year as a four-digit string in `birth_date`.
Render this document first, then run each analysis in 02–11.

## 1 Setup and generation parameters

Fix the random number generator and seed.

```{r}
#| label: setup
library(tidyverse)
library(pins)

# Specify the relative path to the replication board.
board <- board_folder("../income_board_replicate")

simulation_seed <- 20261020L
# The second threshold in 06 reaches rank 300,000. The next growth rate must also be positive.
n_individuals <- 1500000L
birth_years <- 1950:2000
income_start_age <- 20L
simulation_years <- 2014:2020
process_years <- (min(birth_years) + income_start_age):max(simulation_years)

# Median initial income at age 20 is 10 million yen. This is not an estimate from actual data.
initial_log_income_location <- log(1e7)
initial_log_income_sd <- 0.1
initial_log_income_scale <- initial_log_income_sd / sqrt(2)
annual_drift <- 0
shock_shape <- 0.55
shock_scale <- 0.06

RNGkind("Mersenne-Twister", "Inversion", "Rejection")
set.seed(simulation_seed)
```

## 2 Synthetic individual attributes and income panel

Individual IDs are sequential numbers prefixed with `SIM`.
Allocate the 1.5 million individuals as evenly as possible across the 51 birth years from 1950 to 2000.
Randomize the assignment of birth years to IDs, keeping birth year and industry fixed for each individual.
Select industry codes from the integers 1111–9999 and store them as four-digit strings.

Let $B_i$ denote individual $i$'s birth year and $A_i=B_i+20$ the first year in which income is generated.
Independently generate the natural logarithm of income in yen at age 20 from a common Laplace distribution, regardless of birth year.

$$L_{i,A_i}\sim\operatorname{Laplace}(m_0,s_0),\qquad m_0=\log(10^7),\qquad s_0=1/\sqrt{2}.$$

Generate annual growth rates independently of initial log income.
From age 21 onward, add a signed Weibull log growth rate once per year.

$$g_{it}=\mu+S_{it}W_{it},\qquad W_{it}\sim\operatorname{Weibull}(a,b),\qquad P(S_{it}=1)=P(S_{it}=-1)=1/2.$$

$$L_{it}=L_{i,A_i}+\sum_{u=A_i+1}^{t}g_{iu},\qquad Y_{it}=\exp(L_{it}),\qquad t\geq A_i.$$

In the year the individual turns 20, the empty sum is defined as zero.
Here, $\mu=0$, $a=0.55$, and $b=0.06$.
For example, log income in 2014 for an individual born in 1950 includes the value at age 20 and 44 growth increments from 1971 to 2014.

```{r}

individual_tb <- tibble(
  id = sprintf("SIM%07d", seq_len(n_individuals)),
  birth_date = as.character(sample(rep(birth_years, length.out = n_individuals))),
  ind_class = sprintf("%04d", sample(1111:9999, n_individuals, replace = TRUE)),
  initial_log_income = initial_log_income_location + initial_log_income_scale *
    sample(c(-1, 1), n_individuals, replace = TRUE) * rexp(n_individuals)
)
start_year <- as.integer(individual_tb$birth_date) + income_start_age
birth_cohort_counts <- individual_tb |> count(birth_date, name = "n_individuals")
stopifnot(diff(range(birth_cohort_counts$n_individuals)) <= 1L)

log_income <- rep(NA_real_, n_individuals)
n_growth_steps <- integer(n_individuals)
annual_tables <- vector("list", length(simulation_years))
for (this_year in process_years) {
  entrants <- which(start_year == this_year)
  log_income[entrants] <- individual_tb$initial_log_income[entrants]

  continuing <- which(start_year < this_year)
  shock <- sample(c(-1, 1), length(continuing), replace = TRUE) *
    rweibull(length(continuing), shape = shock_shape, scale = shock_scale)
  log_income[continuing] <- log_income[continuing] + annual_drift + shock
  n_growth_steps[continuing] <- n_growth_steps[continuing] + 1L

  active <- which(start_year <= this_year)
  stopifnot(
    all(n_growth_steps[active] == this_year - start_year[active]),
    all(log_income[entrants] == individual_tb$initial_log_income[entrants]),
    all(is.finite(log_income[active])),
    all(is.na(log_income[start_year > this_year]))
  )

  if (this_year %in% simulation_years) {
    annual_tables[[match(this_year, simulation_years)]] <- individual_tb[active, ] |>
      transmute(id, year = as.character(this_year), birth_date, ind_class,
                main_var = exp(log_income[active]))
  }
}
sample_size_tb <- bind_rows(annual_tables)
rm(annual_tables, individual_tb, start_year, log_income, n_growth_steps,
   entrants, continuing, active, shock)
gc(verbose = FALSE)

sample_size_tb |> head(10)

```

The only income variable in `sample_size_tb` is `main_var`; use it to construct `sample_growth_tb` as follows.

## 3 Growth

Calculate $g_{i,t,s}=\log(Y_{it})-\log(Y_{is})$ for six annual periods (2014–15 through 2019–20) and five periods starting in 2014 (2014–16 through 2014–20).
Here, $Y$ is income in yen (`main_var`), and multiyear growth rates are not annualized.

First verify that ID–year combinations are unique, then create combinations of IDs and the 11 growth periods.
Join beginning-of-period income `pre_income` and end-of-period income `post_income` to each row, and store their log difference as `growth`.
Exclude rows with missing or nonfinite growth rates, including periods in which income is unavailable because the individual is under 20 at the beginning or end.

For birth year `birth_date` and industry `ind_class`, use the attributes from the first year in which each ID appears in `sample_size_tb`.
Create `sample_growth_tb` with these attributes and beginning- and end-of-period incomes.

```{r}
growth_f <- function(sample_size_tb) {

  stopifnot(!anyDuplicated(sample_size_tb[c("id", "year")]))

  # Six annual growth periods and five growth periods starting in 2014.
  periods <- tibble(
    post_year = as.character(c(2020:2015, 2016:2020)),
    pre_year = as.character(c(2019:2014, rep(2014, 5)))
  ) |>
    mutate(year = str_c(
      "g_", str_sub(post_year, 3, 4), "_", str_sub(pre_year, 3, 4)
    ))

  income_tb <- sample_size_tb |> select(id, year, main_var)
  attributes_tb <- sample_size_tb |>
    select(id, birth_date, ind_class) |>
    distinct(id, .keep_all = TRUE)

  # Arrange periods for each ID in the same order as in the original code.
  expand_grid(id = unique(sample_size_tb$id), year = periods$year) |>
    left_join(periods, by = "year") |>
    left_join(
      income_tb |> rename(pre_year = year, pre_income = main_var),
      by = c("id", "pre_year")
    ) |>
    left_join(
      income_tb |> rename(post_year = year, post_income = main_var),
      by = c("id", "post_year")
    ) |>
    mutate(growth = log(post_income) - log(pre_income)) |>
    filter(is.finite(growth)) |>
    left_join(attributes_tb, by = "id") |>
    select(id, year, growth, birth_date, ind_class, pre_income, post_income)
}

sample_growth_tb <- growth_f(sample_size_tb)

sample_growth_tb |> head(10)
```

## 4 Saving the data

Save `sample_size_tb` and `sample_growth_tb` to the board.

```{r}

board |> pin_write(sample_size_tb, "sample_size_tb", type = "qs2")
board |> pin_write(sample_growth_tb, "sample_growth_tb", type = "qs2")

```
